messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ahmed, a 56‑year‑old social‑media manager from a close‑knit Middle Eastern family, arrived at the clinic with a score of 48 on the PTSD checklist, a figure that made him feel both overwhelmed and resigned. He had spent the past few months in a careful routine of avoidance and hypervigilance, yet the weight of his memories pressed on him each night, preventing sleep and clouding the conversations with his wife. The reason he finally sought help was a nagging fear that the constant scanning of his surroundings would one day catch him off‑guard, and that his inability to relax would erode the stability of his marriage and career. The trigger that set this cycle in motion was a protest in his city that night, when a group of teenagers was stopped by a squad of police officers. Ahmed was standing in the crowd, hands clasped behind his back, when a cop’s baton cracked the air and a fellow protester was shoved into a glass storefront. The officer’s hand clamped into Ahmed’s wrist, forcing him into a handcuff, and a hot, metallic sting ran through the strap against his skin. The smell of gun oil and the crack of metal filled the air. He heard the officers’ shouts, the thudding of boots, and the distant siren wail. In that instant, he tasted a bitter metallic taste that later returned whenever he tried to think about that night. That night’s event planted deep negative appraisals in Ahmed. He could no longer trust that people, especially those in authority, were reliable; the violence seemed to contradict everything he believed about safety and fairness. He felt that the world had become a dangerous place, one where strangers could turn violence on an unsuspecting citizen at any moment. These appraisals were not abstract thoughts; they made the idea of walking down a familiar street feel like stepping into a trap. Because of the distrust he now held, Ahmed began to perceive every street corner, every passing vehicle, as a potential threat. The memory of the officer’s handcuff, the taste of metal, the sharp sting of fear, kept replaying in his mind and intensified that sense of danger. Each time he recalled that night, the memory’s vividness triggered a surge of rage that surged through him like a flash of electricity. The memory’s taste of bitterness seeped into his senses, reminding him that the world could hurt him without warning. The intensity of that threat made it impossible for him to relax, even in the quiet of his own bedroom, and he spent hours planning escape routes for even the slightest sign of police presence. The persistent threat of violence also hardened his negative appraisal that the world was unsafe. In response to this escalating threat, Ahmed turned to maladaptive strategies. He avoided any content that could stir even a fleeting emotion; he stopped watching news stories or documentaries about police violence and deleted any articles that reminded him of the night. He began to constantly scan his surroundings, his eyes darting to each shadow or flash of light as if it could be the next officer. He avoided all feelings, both positive and negative, fearing that any emotional surge could trigger panic. These avoidance behaviors made it easier for his negative appraisals to dominate his thinking, reinforcing his belief that the world was dangerous and that he was untrustworthy, since he would be seen as fragile if he did not keep his emotions at bay. The avoidance did not help the memory. Each time Ahmed forced himself to stay away from triggers, he pushed the memory further into his mind, only to encounter it again in flashes that were both vivid and intensely angry. The act of avoidance made the memory feel like a locked door that he could not open. In trying to block the recollection, he actually allowed the taste of metal to return, keeping the memory fresh and potent. And every time the memory returned with a wave of rage, it further entrenched his belief that he had violated his own values by failing to stay safe and that the world remained a hostile place. These maladaptive strategies seeped into his professional life. As a social‑media manager, Ahmed was expected to curate content that could include political or social issues. Instead, he avoided any campaign that involved police or protests, fearing that the content would trigger a flood of negative emotions. The avoidance made his work feel tedious and unfulfilling, and he began to feel guilt and shame at the thought of disappointing his team. At home, his wife noticed that Ahmed was increasingly preoccupied with his phone, checking notifications for threats and avoiding conversations that might bring up feelings. Their intimacy suffered; he could not relax with her or even engage in light talk without his mind drifting to possible danger. The weight of these intertwined dynamics became too much to bear. Ahmed’s fear that he would one day fail to protect himself or his family, coupled with a sense that he could not enjoy the normalcy of his job or home life, pushed him toward the clinic. He arrived with a deep hope to break the loop, to learn to let go of the taste of metal that lingered in his tongue, to trust again in people, and to feel calm and present when he stood at a crosswalk or sat with his wife. What frightened him most was the possibility that the cycle might never end, that each step forward would be undermined by a flashback or a perceived threat. What he most hoped for was a chance to finally turn his fear into a safe, controlled awareness, and to reclaim the trust he had lost in the world.
